name: FasciaBlaster

lead: The FasciaBlaster is a self-massage device invented by Ashley Black. It is a long plastic bar with blunt, claw-like protrusions that users glide over oiled skin, with the stated goal of smoothing cellulite, easing stiffness and improving circulation.

The company describes the tool as breaking up adhesions in fascia, the connective tissue under the skin. Outside experts have questioned that explanation, and the one published study of cellulite use was small and partly funded by the company.

paras: Users apply oil or lotion and drag the tool in strokes over the target area, such as thighs and buttocks. Smaller versions exist for the face and hands. The company sells oils and educational material alongside the tools, and treatment is repeated over weeks.

Bruising is the most-cited effect; Black has described it as a sign the treatment is working, while a Stanford surgeon quoted by The New York Times states a bruise does not show fascia has been broken. Users have also reported inflammation, nausea and other symptoms, and class-action lawsuits were filed in 2017.

Deep massage of skin and underlying tissue
angle.text: People use it to smooth dimpled areas on thighs and buttocks and to get a firmer-looking contour. The company says the strokes release fascial adhesions that cause the dimpling.

lead: The FasciaBlaster is a handheld self-massage tool, invented by American entrepreneur Ashley Black, built from plastic with blunt claw-like protrusions [1]. Users glide it over oiled skin, most often on thighs, buttocks and abdomen, to reduce the look of cellulite and loosen tissue they consider tight [1][2].

Black has said the tool was designed in 2014 after her own health problems and years of work with clients; she filed a design patent in February 2014, granted in August 2015, and announced the product by press release in November 2014 [1]. Wikipedia reports an earlier marketing name, Lumpbuster, in 2012 [2]. Variants include a Mini and tools for the face [1].

The company promotes the tool within a system it calls fasciology. Critics and clinicians quoted in press coverage dispute the claims about breaking up fascia, and a single industry-funded study is the main published research [2].

paras: The original tool is a roughly two-foot bar with large claws, with smaller models for targeted areas and the face [1]. The manufacturer recommends oils or lotions sold by the company for glide [1].

Ashley Black, who describes herself as a fasciologist, founded FasciAnatomy and says her interest began with chronic pain after a severe infection [1]. The device was first sold as the Lumpbuster in 2012 according to Wikipedia, and then as the FasciaBlaster [2].
The company claims the tool breaks up fascial adhesions to reduce cellulite and pain [1]. Black has presented bruising as a sign of effectiveness and compared it to cupping [2].
A 2023 New York Times piece stated that no evidence supports fascia blasting, and a Stanford surgeon said a bruise does not mean fascia has been broken up [2].

Users have reported severe bruising, inflammation, nausea and menstrual changes, and some filed complaints with the FDA [2]. In 2017 the company updated its terms of use with warnings about vomiting, hormone changes and headaches [2].
Two proposed class actions filed in 2017 were consolidated as Elson v. Black in 2018, and in January 2023 the Fifth Circuit reversed the dismissal of two claims [2].

A 2019 study in Cogent Medicine, partly funded by Black's company, followed 33 women over 12 weeks and concluded the tool may be a viable method for cellulite, while also reporting irritability, nausea, headaches and bruising [2].

lore.intro: Marketing and fan communities present fascia work as a route to smooth skin and pain relief [1].
